clue.text: Pub against City in needle match

indicators.note: one thing set against another sits right beside it, so the two pieces are placed side by side

parts.note: your local is the pub nearest home
Derby is a city in the English Midlands

explanation.surface: Fans of a pub team and a city team meet in a grudge game.
explanation.walkthrough: A needle match is a fiercely contested game; a local derby is one between two nearby rival teams.
explanation.definitionFit: A game between neighbouring rivals is usually bitter, which is exactly what a needle match describes.

clue.text: Boat set afloat

definitions.meaning: second meaning: to put a newly built vessel into the water

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one picture, a boat being floated, but the word is both the vessel and the act.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch is a motor vessel, and to launch a ship is to slide it into the water for the first time.

clue.text: Poles caught sabre dancing

parts.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and change places, giving a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: People from Poland spotted performing a sword dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like Polish people, but it means long wooden shafts. A caber is the tree trunk tossed at Scottish Highland games.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabers are the heavy tapered wooden poles thrown end over end at Highland games.

clue.text: Ageing, as the walrus undoubtedly is

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an idiom for growing old
second meaning taken literally: a walrus has huge tusks

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom comes from horses, whose gums recede with age so their teeth look longer; a walrus, with its great tusks, fits the phrase literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone getting old, and literally fits an animal with very large tusks.

clue.text: Former church leader's first to stand out

parts.note: ex- means former
CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: first points at the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the first letter of leader

explanation.surface: An ex-bishop is the first to rise to prominence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'church leader' wants to be one figure, but it splits: church gives CE, and leader's first gives L.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to be exceptionally good, so to be outstanding among others.

clue.text: Annual dinner of beef 'Santa' may provide

indicators.note: the letters may supply the answer once put into a different arrangement

parts.note: the letters of beef and Santa

explanation.surface: Father Christmas might lay on a beef dinner at the yearly festive meal.
explanation.walkthrough: A beanfeast was originally the annual dinner an employer gave the workforce; now any jolly celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a beanfeast was the yearly meal an employer laid on for workers, hence any festive spread.

clue.text: Animal kept for breeding gets endless attention

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the next word is cut off

parts.note: close study is careful attention

explanation.surface: A prize breeding animal is pampered with constant care.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last letter of STUDY.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is a male horse or other beast retained specifically to sire offspring.

clue.text: Hothead showing sign of emotion at opponent's ground

parts.note: a tear shed when moved
a team playing at its opponent's ground is playing away

explanation.surface: An angry fan gets emotional at an away match.
explanation.definitionFit: A tearaway is a reckless, impetuous young person, a hothead who acts without thinking.

clue.text: Drop iron?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fall or reduction
second meaning, punning: to ... is to remove creases, as ironing does

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: split as DE-CREASE, the word means take the creases out, which is what you do with an iron.
explanation.definitionFit: A decrease is a drop in amount; read as de-crease it means smoothing out wrinkles.

clue.text: Admitted as a barrister shouted for drinks?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: formally qualified to practise as a barrister
second meaning, taken literally: summoned over to the pub counter

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the literal reading: to be called to the bar is also to be summoned to where drinks are served.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a lawyer becomes a barrister by the formal ceremony known by this phrase.

clue.text: Living in a town in Darfur, Bangladeshi

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of words that follows, spanning the gap between them

parts.note: the end of Darfur and the start of Bangladeshi

explanation.surface: Describes someone from Bangladesh who has settled in a Sudanese town.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban is the adjective for city or town life, as opposed to rural living.

clue.text: Almost risk bringing in Arab coach

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside, so one piece goes within the other
almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the word for risk is dropped

parts.note: to chance something is to risk it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A daring venture to smuggle a man from Arabia aboard a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: A charabanc is an old open-topped motor coach used for day outings, a word borrowed from French char-a-bancs, carriage with benches.
explanation.definitionFit: A charabanc is an early motor bus used for sightseeing trips, a kind of coach.

clue.text: Stimulating drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old sense of the adjective, invigorating the heart
second meaning: a sweet fruit concentrate diluted with water

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase, a pick-me-up drink, but splits into two senses; the adjective sense now usually means warm and friendly, while its origin is heart-reviving.
explanation.definitionFit: The word came from Latin for heart: a heart-reviving medicine, then a sweet diluted beverage.

clue.text: Leaves foil, crumpled with time

indicators.note: crumpled foil is screwed up out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: A scrunched sheet of kitchen foil that has been left lying around for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb, someone leaving the foil, but it is the noun plural and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Foliage is the collective term for a plant's leaves.

clue.text: Flag showing major shipping hazards

parts.note: a star player or attraction is the major one
sandbars are submerged ridges ships can run aground on

explanation.surface: A banner marking out the worst dangers to vessels at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The word boundaries move: the wordplay is two words that respace into three. The Stars and Bars was the first flag of the American Confederacy.
explanation.definitionFit: Stars and Bars is the name of the first national banner of the Confederate States of America.

clue.text: Produces a meal at short notice — smashing result, with drink later

definitions.text: Produces a meal at short notice

indicators.note: later says this piece comes after the other in the answer
smashing something breaks it apart, so these letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
to sup is to drink, or a sup is a mouthful

explanation.surface: A cook whips up a quick dinner with great success, followed by a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashing result' reads as praise for the meal, but smashing is the anagram signal working on result.
explanation.definitionFit: To rustle up food is an idiom for preparing it quickly from whatever is to hand.

clue.text: One holds a sword — he won't strike poet

parts.note: a scab is a worker who refuses to join a strike
a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A swordsman who declines to fight, paired with a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'won't strike' beside a sword suggests not attacking, but it means crossing a picket line.
explanation.definitionFit: A scabbard is the sheath that encloses a sword's blade when it is not in use.

clue.text: Fearless, I unwisely printed

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: done unwisely means done badly, so the letters fall into a different order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A bold journalist admits publishing something rash.
explanation.definitionFit: Intrepid is a synonym for bold or brave, describing someone who shows no fear.

clue.text: There's talk of a bit of trouble during change-over

indicators.note: something happening during another event falls inside it, so these letters sit within the other word

parts.note: a conversion is a change from one form to another
taken as written

indicators.note: only a small bit of the word is wanted, here its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of trouble

explanation.surface: Gossip about a minor problem that cropped up during a shift handover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change-over' looks like a shift handover in the surface, but it is a noun for transformation.
explanation.definitionFit: Conversation is informal spoken exchange between people, which is what talk means as a noun.

clue.text: Socialist premier in tabloid

parts.note: red is the colour of socialism
premier means top, first-ranked

explanation.surface: A left-wing prime minister appears in a scandal sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'premier' looks like a prime minister, but it is the adjective meaning best. A red-top is a British mass-market tabloid, named for its red masthead.
explanation.definitionFit: British popular tabloid newspapers such as The Sun carry red mastheads, so they are called red-tops.

clue.text: Odd scene involving a session with a spiritualist

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one piece is wrapped round the other
odd means strange or out of place, so these letters are put into an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A strange scene at a sitting with a medium.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of scene become SENCE, then A goes inside after SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A seance is a meeting at which a medium attempts to contact the dead.

clue.text: Bird ran off in stadium

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: a bowl is a large amphitheatre-style stadium

indicators.note: off means gone wrong or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A bird darted away inside a sports ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ran off' reads as a bird fleeing; instead the letters of ran are mixed and placed in BOWL.
explanation.definitionFit: The barn owl is a pale species of owl, a bird often nesting in farm buildings.

clue.text: A permit held by the sportsman

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something held by another thing is gripped within it, so these letters go inside the next word

parts.note: taken as written
to let is to permit

explanation.surface: A licence is in the possession of a sporting man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' looks like a mere article, but it supplies letters of its own and acts as the container.
explanation.definitionFit: An athlete is someone who competes in sport, especially track and field events.

clue.text: A bishop, as seen in wall hanging

parts.note: taken as written
RR is Right Reverend, a bishop's title
taken as written

explanation.surface: A churchman's portrait woven into a tapestry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' only links the wordplay to the definition; it is not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An arras is a rich tapestry hung on a wall, named after the French town famous for weaving them.

clue.text: Mushy peas and tripe starter

indicators.note: something mushy has been mashed into a pulp, so these letters are reshaped

parts.note: the letters of peas and tripe, without the and

explanation.surface: A first course of mushy peas with tripe, a famously unglamorous northern English dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' joins the two fodder words and contributes no letters. Mushy peas are mashed marrowfat peas, a British chip-shop side.
explanation.definitionFit: An appetiser is a small dish served at the start of a meal, the course also called a starter.

clue.text: Bar, stifling to staff

indicators.note: to stifle is to smother by wrapping round, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: to bar is to ban
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bar so hot and airless it suffocates the employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like workers in the bar, but it is a stick, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A baton is a short stick or rod, such as a conductor's or a relay runner's, so a staff.

clue.text: The queen of Carthage accomplished nothing

parts.note: to have done a thing is to have accomplished it
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A legendary ruler of an ancient city is dismissed as having achieved nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido was the legendary founder and ruler of Carthage, abandoned by Aeneas in Virgil's epic.

clue.text: What Bloomingdale's always has in?

parts.note: surface reading: a stock item that the New York department store never runs out of
setter's reading: the punctuation mark that is always inside the store's written name

explanation.walkthrough: The clue pretends to ask about merchandise; 'has in' really means contains in its spelling, and the name Bloomingdale's is always written with a mark before the final s.
explanation.definitionFit: The store's possessive name always contains that raised comma-like punctuation mark between its e and s.
